hints: Think about what makes the d block special, focus on the d orbitals in the ion formed, not just in the neutral atom.
walkthrough:
Pin down the key test**
Picture cobalt as $\text{Co}$ with configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^74s^2$. When it loses electrons it forms $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($3d^7$) and $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$). Both have a d subshell that is neither empty nor full, and both ions are stable and common. That is the whole test.
Final answer: A transition element is an element that forms one or more stable ions with partially filled (incomplete) d orbitals.

hints: Recall the three classic reaction types for $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$: $\text{OH}^-$ gives a hydroxide precipitate, excess $\text{Cl}^-$ gives a tetrahedral chloro complex, excess $\text{NH}_3$ gives an ammine complex by ligand exchange.
Work out charge balance and coordination number for each: hydroxide is neutral $\text{Co(OH)}_2$, chloride complex is $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, ammine complex is $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Sort A as acid base precipitation**
With $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$, water ligands are deprotonated and displaced to give the neutral hydroxide. Think $\text{Co}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_2$. So A is $\text{Co(OH)}_2$, often written hydrated as $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2$.

Sort B and C as ligand exchange**
Excess $\text{Cl}^-$ replaces all six waters to give the tetrahedral complex $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$. Check charge: $+2 + 4(-1) = -2$. Excess $\text{NH}_3$ replaces all six waters to give the octahedral complex $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$. In air this Co(II) ammine is readily oxidised to $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, so both are accepted.

Final answer: A = $\text{Co(OH)}_2$ or $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2$
B = $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$
C = $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ (oxidised in air to $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ also accepted)

hints: Start from the very familiar starting ion $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ seen in hydrated cobalt salts, recall its characteristic pink colour.
Link the other two to classic colour changes: $\text{Cl}^-$ complex is the deep blue of dry cobalt chloride paper, $\text{NH}_3$ complex gives a brown to yellow solution.
walkthrough:
Anchor the starting colour**
$[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ is the pink ion you see in aqueous cobalt(II) chloride or nitrate. Keep that as your reference.

Recall the ligand change colours**
Changing ligands changes d orbital splitting and hence the colour of light absorbed. The tetrahedral $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ is intensely blue. The hexaammine product C gives a brown to yellow to orange solution. Learn these as a set: pink to blue to brown.

Final answer: $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ pink
solution of B blue
solution of C brown / yellow / orange

hints: Remember every electrode potential is a comparison, think which reference electrode is defined as 0.00 V.
List the standard conditions that must be stated for ions, gases and temperature to make the comparison fair.
walkthrough:
See it as a comparison**
You can never measure one half-cell alone. You always join it to the standard hydrogen electrode, $\text{Pt} | \text{H}_2 | \text{H}^+$, which is assigned $E^\ominus = 0.00 \text{ V}$. The voltage you read is the standard electrode potential of your half-cell.

Add the standard state rules**
For the value to be standard, all species must be in standard states: dissolved ions at $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, any gases at $1 \text{ atm}$, and $T = 298 \text{ K}$. Without quoting these, the definition is incomplete.

Final answer: The emf (potential) of a half-cell connected to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) under standard conditions.
Standard conditions: ion concentration $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, gas pressure $1 \text{ atm}$ (101 kPa) and temperature 298 K.

hints: Decide for each half-cell whether the metal itself can conduct electrons or whether both species are in solution and need an inert carrier.
walkthrough:
Choose active versus inert**
For $\text{Co}^{2+}/\text{Co}$ the solid metal Co is present, so it acts as its own electrode and electron conductor. For $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ both ions are in solution with no solid metal, so you need an inert conductor that does not react, platinum (or graphite) is ideal.

Final answer: $\text{Co}^{2+}/\text{Co}$: Co (cobalt) metal electrode
$\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$: Pt (or carbon / graphite) inert electrode

hints: Use $E^\ominus$ values to spot which is oxidised and which is reduced: $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ (+0.77 V) will be reduced, Co will be oxidised.
walkthrough:
Combine to cancel electrons**
Write the halves: $\text{Co} \rightarrow \text{Co}^{2+} + 2e^-$ (oxidation) and $\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$ (reduction). Multiply the iron half by 2 to balance the 2 electrons from cobalt, then add: $\text{Co} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Co}^{2+} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}$.

hints: Apply $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{positive} - E^\ominus_{negative}$ using +0.77 V for iron and -0.28 V for cobalt.
walkthrough:
Subtract carefully**
$$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode}$$
$$= +0.77 - (-0.28) = +1.05 \text{ V}$$
The double negative makes it addition. The positive sign confirms the reaction in (ii) is feasible under standard conditions.
Final answer: $E^\ominus_{cell} = 0.77 - (-0.28) = +1.05 \text{ V}$

hints: Identify $E^\ominus = -0.28 \text{ V}$, $z = 2$ for $\text{Co}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Co}$, and $[\text{Co}^{2+}] = 0.050$ in $E = E^\ominus + (0.059/z)\log[\text{Co}^{2+}]$.
walkthrough:
Substitute into Nernst**
$$E = E^\ominus + (0.059/z)\log[\text{Co}^{2+}]$$
$$E = -0.28 + (0.059/2)\log(0.050)$$
$\log(0.050) = -1.30$, so $(0.0295 \times -1.30) = -0.038$. Hence $E = -0.28 -0.038 = -0.32 \text{ V}$. Lower $[\text{Co}^{2+}]$ shifts the $\text{Co}^{2+}/\text{Co}$ equilibrium to the left, making the electrode more negative.

hints: Think how $E_{cell} = E_{Fe} - E_{Co}$ changes when $E_{Co}$ becomes more negative while $E_{Fe}$ stays standard.
walkthrough:
Track the subtraction**
$E_{cell} = E_{Fe} - E_{Co}$. $E_{Co}$ has fallen from $-0.28$ to $-0.32 \text{ V}$. Subtracting a more negative number gives a larger value: $0.77 - (-0.32) = 1.09 \text{ V}$. So $E_{cell}$ becomes more positive than $E^\ominus_{cell}$ in (d)(iii).

hints: Compare $E^\ominus$ values: $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is +0.77 V, strong enough to oxidise V all the way past $\text{V}^{2+}$, $\text{V}^{3+}$ and $\text{VO}^{2+}$ to the highest accessible state with excess oxidant.

With excess $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, vanadium(0) is oxidised to $\text{VO}^{2+}$ (V in +4 state), now balance O with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and H with $\text{H}^+$ alongside the $4e^-$ taken by $4\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
walkthrough:
Pick the final vanadium product**
Excess $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is a strong oxidant and will drive V(0) to its most oxidised form available in the Data Booklet list, which is the oxovanadium(IV) ion, $\text{VO}^{2+}$ where V is +4. This involves loss of 4 electrons.

Build the balanced redox equation**
Reduction: $\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$, multiply by 4. Oxidation: $\text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$. Note you need $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply O and $\text{H}^+$ to balance H. Adding halves to cancel $4e^-$ gives:
$$4\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 4\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+$$
Check atoms and charge: $12+$ both sides, 4 Fe, 1 V, 1 O, 2 H balanced.

Final answer: Vanadium is oxidised to $\text{VO}^{2+}$
$4\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 4\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+$
